script.opening: (Relaxed, slightly dismissive, keen to keep it short.) "Morning. I know I'm booked in after the A&E thing, but honestly it was a one-off — I just had a bad cold and my chest flared. I'm completely back to normal now. I don't really think there's much to discuss; I don't want to make a big deal of it."

facts.text: "The cold started, I got wheezy, and I kept using the blue one. When it stopped helping, I went in." Three days of worsening wheeze; on the night, couldn't finish sentences, used the blue inhaler "loads, maybe 20 puffs". Partner drove him to A&E at 3 am. Nebulisers, steroids, discharged after 6 hours.
If asked gently: "Yeah… it was scary, to be fair. I didn't want to make a fuss."
If asked non-judgementally: "Honestly? On and off. When I felt fine I didn't see the point." Fluticasone preventer — collected 3 times in the last year.
"Now and then. I didn't really keep track" — about 3–4 times a week before the cold; 2 inhalers in the last 3 months.
"Not that I remember" — no previous admissions or intensive care. One previous course of steroid tablets 2 years ago.
"Yeah, I finished them" (5 days prednisolone). Now: no night waking, mild wheeze running for the bus.
"Colds, mainly. I don't really notice anything else." Doesn't smoke; works in a bakery (flour dust) — hasn't noticed a pattern. No pets. No NSAIDs.
Asthma since age 10. No action plan. Not had flu or COVID vaccine this year. No allergies. Lives with partner, Ama.

Minimising: "If you think it's worth it." If asked what being asthmatic means to him: "I don't want to be one of those sickly people with inhalers everywhere. I'm 31. I just want to get on with things." Sobered by the risk: "So it could happen again." Open to a single inhaler: "One inhaler I could live with." Technique if asked to show: "Shake, puff, breathe" — fires and inhales out of sync. Admits: "I didn't really know when to go last time."

ice.ideas: "It was a one-off caused by a cold."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — it frightened him more than he admits; embarrassed about not taking his preventer; doesn't want to see himself as "sickly".

cues: "It was a one-off." — minimising a serious attack.
"I didn't want to make a fuss." — he waited too long.
"When I felt fine I didn't see the point." — the adherence truth, if asked kindly.

checkpoints.text: Recognises that a recent ATTACK requiring A&E/oral steroids is a MAJOR risk factor for a future severe/fatal attack — treating the post-attack review as high-value and countering the minimisation
Reconstructs the attack and elicits the ADHERENCE TRUTH NON-JUDGEMENTALLY — preventer use before the attack, technique, running out, reliever over-reliance, and any delay in seeking help
Reassesses current control and documents RISK FACTORS (previous severe/ICU attacks, multiple A&E/admissions, high SABA use, poor adherence, no action plan, smoking, allergy/anxiety, social factors)

OPTIMISES treatment in the NICE NG245 order — adherence, inhaler TECHNIQUE and triggers first, then low-dose MART if not controlled on low-dose ICS plus SABA — confirms the steroid course completed (dose per BNF), addresses reliever over-reliance

Co-creates a PERSONALISED ASTHMA ACTION PLAN, addresses triggers (viral illness, smoking, allergens, occupational) and vaccination, and arranges STRUCTURED post-exacerbation follow-up (NICE QS25: within 2 working days of emergency care, so acknowledges this review is late; then a review a few weeks after any change) plus ongoing review
Validates that he feels well now while gently countering the "just a cold/no fuss" minimisation, and surfaces the adherence story without judgement so he engages honestly
Explains why the review matters (future-attack risk) in a way that motivates rather than frightens, and checks understanding of the plan and technique

Safety-nets and follows up: attack red flags and emergency advice, the action plan, optimised regimen with review of adherence/control, structured post-exacerbation recall, and engagement secured — not a colluding "nothing to discuss" review

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you came, and I get that you feel fine now — that’s good. But I want to be honest: needing A&E and steroids means your asthma was genuinely dangerous that day, not just a cold. Understanding why is the best way to make sure it doesn’t happen again."

"Talk me through it — how did it build up, and how long before you got help? … And in the weeks before, were you taking the preventer regularly, or had it slipped? Honestly — loads of people drift off it when they feel well, it’s really common, I’m not telling you off."

"So the brown inhaler had been on and off. That’s really useful to know, because that’s often the thread behind an attack — the inflammation builds up quietly while you feel okay, then a cold tips it over. We can fix that."
"Let’s get you on a regimen that’s easier to stick to — ideally one inhaler that’s both preventer and reliever — and check your technique now. Did you finish the steroid course? Good."

"I’ll write you a personal action plan: what your normal is, the early warning signs, when to step up, and exactly when to get emergency help. Having this in writing genuinely reduces the risk of another bad attack."

"I’d like to see you again soon to check how you’re doing on the new inhaler, in a few weeks — these reviews after an attack really matter, and ideally we’d have spoken within a couple of days of A&E, so I’m sorry it’s been ten. And if you’re ever breathless at rest or can’t speak in full sentences, that’s 999. Deal?"

f.learning: The post-attack asthma review is high-value because a recent ATTACK requiring A&E or oral steroids is one of the STRONGEST predictors of a future severe or fatal attack — so the patient’s "it was just a cold, I’m fine, no fuss" minimisation must be gently but clearly countered: needing A&E and steroids means the asthma was dangerously out of control, and understanding why prevents the next event. Reconstruct the attack (how it built, what he did, any delay in seeking help — common and dangerous) and elicit the ADHERENCE TRUTH NON-JUDGEMENTALLY — whether the preventer was being taken regularly, technique, running out, reliever over-reliance — normalising that many people drift off the preventer when well, to get the real rather than defensive story. Reassess current control and document risk factors for future attacks (previous near-fatal/ICU attacks, multiple A&E/admissions, high SABA use, poor adherence, no action plan, smoking, allergy/anxiety, social factors). OPTIMISE treatment in the NICE NG245 order — address adherence, inhaler technique, triggers and alternative diagnoses first, then move from regular low-dose ICS plus SABA to low-dose ICS-formoterol MART (moderate-dose MART and specialist advice if still uncontrolled), confirm the steroid course completed (dose per BNF), and address reliever over-reliance (MHRA, April 2025: no SABA without an ICS). Co-create a PERSONALISED ASTHMA ACTION PLAN (recognise deterioration, when to step up, when to seek emergency help — written plans reduce attacks and deaths), address triggers and flu vaccine eligibility (Green Book chapter 19), and arrange STRUCTURED post-exacerbation FOLLOW-UP (NICE QS25: general practice follow-up within 2 working days of emergency care, then a review a few weeks after any treatment change, with ongoing annual review). The communication skill is validating that he feels well now, surfacing the adherence story without judgement, and converting a minimised event into engagement and a concrete plan rather than colluding with "nothing to discuss".

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG245 (asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · [2] NICE QS25 (asthma, 2013, updated 2018) · [3] RCP National Review of Asthma Deaths, Why asthma still kills (2014) · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): SABA overuse in asthma · [5] UKHSA Green Book chapter 19 (influenza)
knowledge.summary: An attack needing A&E and oral steroids is uncontrolled asthma and one of the strongest markers of future severe attacks. Find out why it happened — especially the preventer story — without blame, then optimise treatment, check technique, write an action plan and arrange proper follow-up. NICE QS25 expects GP follow-up within 2 working days of emergency care, so this review is already late.

points.t: A recent attack needing emergency care or oral steroids predicts further attacks. NICE NG245 [1] counts any exacerbation needing oral corticosteroids as uncontrolled asthma. The National Review of Asthma Deaths [3] found many deaths followed missed warning signs, poor preventer use and no action plan.

NICE QS25 [2] statement 4: people treated in an emergency care setting for an asthma attack are followed up by their general practice within 2 working days of discharge, to explore why it happened and reduce the risk of another. A review at 10 days is late: acknowledge it and check the practice’s recall system.

Triggers (here a viral cold), how quickly it built, reliever use before the attack, how long before help was sought, and preventer use in the preceding weeks. Check prescription records for preventer and reliever issues, oral steroid courses and previous attendances (NICE NG245 [1]).

NICE NG245 [1]: before changing medicines address adherence, inhaler technique, triggers and alternative diagnoses. For people aged 12 and over not controlled on regular low-dose ICS plus SABA, consider low-dose MART with ICS/formoterol. MHRA (April 2025) [4]: do not prescribe a SABA without an ICS.

Confirm the prednisolone course was completed as directed and ask about side effects. Doses per BNF. More than one course a year is a marker for review and, with repeated courses, for bone health and specialist input.

A written personalised asthma action plan (NICE QS25 [2]) covering usual treatment, early warning signs such as a cold with rising reliever need, how to increase treatment, and when to call 999. Build the plan around what happened this time.

Check flu vaccine eligibility under Green Book chapter 19 [5], smoking and other triggers, and book the next review. Refer for specialist assessment if control remains poor despite good adherence and technique (NICE NG245 [1]).

dg.d: Open start; validated that he feels well before explaining why the review matters.
Not wanting to be a “sickly person”, wish not to fuss, smoking and triggers.
Prescription record review of preventer and reliever issues; technique on video; validated control questionnaire; objective tests if uncertain.
Viral trigger on a background of under-treated inflammation versus poor technique, other triggers or an alternative diagnosis.
Asked about previous attacks, admissions, ICU, delayed help-seeking and completion of the steroid course.
Named uncontrolled asthma with a recent attack and an increased risk of another.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

dg.t: Finishes data gathering in good time
dg.d: History, ICE, psychosocial context and red-flag screen completed by ~6–7 minutes, leaving time for explanation and a shared plan.

cm.d: Low-dose MART (NICE NG245); technique corrected; personalised written action plan.
Triggers, smoking and flu vaccine eligibility; recognised the late review against NICE QS25.
Same-day and 999 triggers; teach-back; review booked in two to four weeks.

cm.t: Uses psychosocial information in the plan
cm.d: Tailored the plan to the patient’s circumstances, beliefs and practical barriers rather than giving a generic plan.

cm.t: Shares risks and safety of options
cm.d: Explained the benefits and risks of the options clearly, as concrete terms or numbers where possible.
Acknowledged autonomy, capacity, confidentiality, safeguarding and any fitness-to-drive/work or duty-of-care implications relevant to this case.
Moved efficiently through the consultation so all key areas were covered within the time without getting stuck.

ro.d: Picked up “I didn’t want to make a fuss” and the fear when the reliever stopped working.
Idea (a one-off cold), concern (being seen as unwell, fuss), expectation (quick review).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — it frightened him more than he admits; embarrassed about not taking his preventer; doesn't want to see himself as "sickly" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hi Kwame, I’m Dr Evans. Thanks for joining. I know you ended up in A&E with your chest recently. How are you doing now?
Honestly, I’m back to normal. It was a one-off — I had a bad cold and my chest flared. I don’t think there’s much to discuss.

I’m really glad you feel better. I won’t keep you longer than we need, but an attack that needs A&E and steroids is worth understanding, so we can stop the next one. Can we go through what happened, look at your inhalers, and make a plan for next time?
model.why: Validates, then gives a clear reason and structure

model.text: If you think it’s worth it.
Talk me through it. How did it build up, and at what point did you decide to go to A&E?
model.why: Reconstructs the attack and the time to seek help

model.text: The cold started, I got wheezy, and I kept using the blue one. When it stopped helping, I went in.
That sounds frightening. When the blue one stopped working, what went through your mind?
model.why: Picks up the emotional cue inside the minimisation

model.text: Yeah… it was scary, to be fair. I didn’t want to make a fuss.

Thanks for saying that. Can I ask about the brown inhaler? A lot of people drift off it when they feel well — it’s really common, and I’m not telling you off. In the weeks before the cold, how often were you taking it?
Honestly? On and off. When I felt fine I didn’t see the point.
That’s really useful, thank you. And before the cold, how often were you using the blue one, and did your chest wake you at night?
Now and then. I didn’t really keep track.
Have you ever needed steroid tablets, A&E or a hospital stay for your asthma before this, or intensive care?
model.why: Past severe attacks — key risk factors

model.text: Not that I remember.
Did you finish the steroid tablets from A&E, and any problems with them?
Yeah, I finished them.
And does anything else set your chest off — and do you smoke or vape?
Colds, mainly. I don’t really notice anything else.
You said you didn’t want to make a fuss, and you’d rather not make a big deal of this. What is it about the fuss you’d rather avoid?
model.why: Explores the hidden agenda behind the minimising

model.text: I don’t want to be one of those sickly people with inhalers everywhere. I’m 31. I just want to get on with things.
That makes complete sense. My aim is the same as yours — less asthma getting in the way, not more.
model.why: Aligns the plan with his goal

model.text: Here’s how I see it. The preventer calms swelling inside the airways that you can’t feel. When it’s taken on and off, that swelling builds quietly, and then a cold tips it over. The blue one opens things up for a while, but it can’t touch the swelling — which is why it stopped working. So this wasn’t just bad luck with a cold.
model.why: Explains the likely mechanism without blame

model.text: So it could happen again.
It could — having one attack like this makes another more likely. The good news is that the things that reduce the risk are simple, and they fit with you not wanting inhalers everywhere.
model.why: Honest about risk, framed to motivate

model.text: One option is a single inhaler that has the preventer and a quick-acting reliever in it. You take it morning and night, and if you’re wheezy you take an extra puff of the same one instead of the blue. So when you reach for relief, you’re treating the swelling too. One inhaler rather than two.
model.why: Offers low-dose MART per NICE NG245

model.text: One inhaler I could live with.
Great. Could you show me how you use your inhaler now, on camera?
Shake, puff, breathe.

Close. Breathe out fully first, then press as you start a slow breath in, and hold for about ten seconds. I’ll also write you an action plan built on what happened: a cold plus needing extra puffs is your early warning, what to do, and when it’s 999.
model.why: Corrects technique and personalises the action plan

model.text: Makes sense. I didn’t really know when to go last time.

That’s what the plan is for. So: if you need extra puffs more and more, or they’re not lasting, contact us the same day. If you’re struggling to talk in sentences, or the inhaler isn’t helping, call 999 — don’t wait.
model.why: Specific red flags linked to his own attack

model.text: Okay. I won’t leave it.
Can you tell me back the plan in your own words?
New single inhaler every day, extra puff when wheezy, action plan, same day if it’s not lasting, 999 if I can’t talk.

Spot on. I’ll see you again in two to four weeks to check how it’s going, and we’ll look at your flu jab. I should say — we ought to have seen you sooner after A&E, and I’m looking at why that didn’t happen. Thanks, Kwame.
model.why: Follow-up, prevention and candour about the delay

social.t: Young adults often resist being seen as ill. Frame treatment as what lets him get on with life; one inhaler can feel less medical than two.
Ask whether the attack affected work; a fit note may be needed if recovery is incomplete (self-certification covers the first 7 days).

legal.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): do not prescribe a SABA without a concomitant ICS.

professional.t: NICE QS25 statement 4: general practice follow-up within 2 working days of emergency care for an asthma attack. A late review is a system issue to reflect on and fix (significant event or audit).
GMC Good medical practice (2024): be open when care falls short. Telling him the review should have been sooner builds trust.

community.t: Community pharmacy New Medicine Service for the new inhaler; Asthma + Lung UK technique videos and action plan templates; practice asthma nurse review.

redFlags: Previous near-fatal attack, ICU or admissions
More than one oral steroid course or A&E attendance a year
Delay in seeking help during attacks
High reliever use, poor preventer use, no action plan
psychosocial: Not wanting to be a “sickly person”
Reluctance to make a fuss, which delayed help
ice: Idea: “A one-off caused by a cold.”
Concern: being seen as unwell; making a fuss
Expectation: a quick review with nothing to change

playbook.diagnosis: “Needing A&E and steroids means your asthma was out of control that day. The likely reason is swelling building up while the preventer was on and off, and the cold tipped it over.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the airway lining like a smouldering fire. The preventer keeps it damped down. When it’s taken on and off, the embers build, and a cold is the gust of wind that sets it alight.”

management.reflectIce: “You don’t want asthma to take over your life — that’s exactly what this plan is for.”
management.psychosocial: Use his wish for less fuss: one inhaler, a simple plan, and clear permission to seek help early next time.
sharedPlan: Low-dose MART with ICS/formoterol (NICE NG245); dose and daily maximum per BNF
Technique corrected; personalised written action plan built around a cold as the trigger
Flu vaccine eligibility; triggers and smoking; review the practice recall process
safetyNet: Same day: rising need for extra puffs or relief not lasting
999: struggling to speak, no response to the inhaler
Review in two to four weeks, then regular review

pitfalls.intro: The trap is a pleasant, short consultation that agrees with “just a cold”. The marks are in treating the attack as a warning, getting the honest preventer story, and leaving him with a plan he will use.

items.fail: Accepting “it was just a cold” and closing in four minutes.
items.why: NICE NG245 counts any attack needing oral steroids as uncontrolled asthma; missing it is unsafe.
items.fix: One sentence of purpose: “An attack like this is worth understanding so we stop the next one.”

items.fail: Asking “Were you taking your preventer?” in a tone that expects a no.
items.why: “Judgemental approach” feedback; he defends rather than discloses.
items.fix: Normalise first: “Lots of people drift off it when they feel well.”

items.fail: Not asking how long he waited before going to A&E.
items.why: Delayed help-seeking is a recurring factor in asthma deaths (NRAD 2014) and must shape the action plan.
items.fix: “At what point did you decide to get help?” Then build the answer into the plan.

items.fail: Doubling the preventer dose without checking technique or adherence.
items.why: NICE NG245: address adherence and technique before changing medicines.
items.fix: Technique check on camera, then low-dose MART.

items.fail: A generic printed action plan handed over without discussion.
items.why: Action plans work when they are personalised and understood.
items.fix: Use his attack: “A cold plus needing extra puffs is your early warning.”

items.fail: No follow-up date — “see you at your annual review”.
items.why: NICE QS25 expects early follow-up after emergency care; a recent attack needs a close review.
items.fix: Book two to four weeks, and acknowledge this review should have been sooner.

timeMap.d: Glad he feels well; give the reason for the review in one sentence.
Build-up, time to help, preventer use before the attack, reliever use, night symptoms, past attacks, steroid course, triggers, smoking.
Not wanting fuss or to be seen as unwell.
Quiet inflammation plus a cold; one attack raises the risk of another.
Low-dose MART, technique, personalised action plan, red flags, teach-back, review, candour about the delay.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “just a cold” and closes quickly; or lectures about adherence and blames him; no action plan, no technique check, no follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Explains why the review matters, elicits preventer use without blame, optimises treatment, gives an action plan and books follow-up.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: reconstructs the attack including the delay in seeking help; links the plan to his wish not to be a “sickly person”; offers low-dose MART as NG245 recommends; builds the action plan around his own early warning signs; notes that follow-up should have been within 2 working days.

avoid.instead: “Lots of people drift off it when they feel well — how often were you taking it?”
avoid.why: Blame produces a defensive answer, not the true story.

avoid.instead: “Needing A&E and steroids means your asthma was genuinely dangerous that day — let’s stop it happening again.”
avoid.why: Honesty with a way forward motivates; fear alone disengages.

avoid.dont: “Glad you’re better — see you at your annual review.”
avoid.instead: “I’d like to see you again in a few weeks to check how the new plan is going.”
avoid.why: A recent attack needs structured follow-up, not annual recall.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG245 (asthma: diagnosis, monitoring and chronic asthma management, 2024, joint with BTS and SIGN) · [2] NICE QS25 (asthma, 2013, updated 2018) · [3] RCP National Review of Asthma Deaths, Why asthma still kills (2014) · [4] MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): SABA overuse in asthma · [5] UKHSA Green Book chapter 19 (influenza)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: An attack needing A&E and oral steroids is uncontrolled asthma and one of the strongest markers of future severe attacks. Find out why it happened — especially the preventer story — without blame, then optimise treatment, check technique, write an action plan and arrange proper follow-up. NICE QS25 expects GP follow-up within 2 working days of emergency care, so this review is already late.

points.t: A recent attack needing emergency care or oral steroids predicts further attacks. NICE NG245 [1] counts any exacerbation needing oral corticosteroids as uncontrolled asthma. The National Review of Asthma Deaths [3] found many deaths followed missed warning signs, poor preventer use and no action plan.

NICE QS25 [2] statement 4: people treated in an emergency care setting for an asthma attack are followed up by their general practice within 2 working days of discharge, to explore why it happened and reduce the risk of another. A review at 10 days is late: acknowledge it and check the practice’s recall system.

Triggers (here a viral cold), how quickly it built, reliever use before the attack, how long before help was sought, and preventer use in the preceding weeks. Check prescription records for preventer and reliever issues, oral steroid courses and previous attendances (NICE NG245 [1]).

NICE NG245 [1]: before changing medicines address adherence, inhaler technique, triggers and alternative diagnoses. For people aged 12 and over not controlled on regular low-dose ICS plus SABA, consider low-dose MART with ICS/formoterol. MHRA (April 2025) [4]: do not prescribe a SABA without an ICS.

Confirm the prednisolone course was completed as directed and ask about side effects. Doses per BNF. More than one course a year is a marker for review and, with repeated courses, for bone health and specialist input.

A written personalised asthma action plan (NICE QS25 [2]) covering usual treatment, early warning signs such as a cold with rising reliever need, how to increase treatment, and when to call 999. Build the plan around what happened this time.

Check flu vaccine eligibility under Green Book chapter 19 [5], smoking and other triggers, and book the next review. Refer for specialist assessment if control remains poor despite good adherence and technique (NICE NG245 [1]).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open start; validated that he feels well before explaining why the review matters.
Not wanting to be a “sickly person”, wish not to fuss, smoking and triggers.
Picked up “I didn’t want to make a fuss” and the fear when the reliever stopped working.
Idea (a one-off cold), concern (being seen as unwell, fuss), expectation (quick review).
Prescription record review of preventer and reliever issues; technique on video; validated control questionnaire; objective tests if uncertain.
Viral trigger on a background of under-treated inflammation versus poor technique, other triggers or an alternative diagnosis.
Asked about previous attacks, admissions, ICU, delayed help-seeking and completion of the steroid course.
Named uncontrolled asthma with a recent attack and an increased risk of another.
Low-dose MART (NICE NG245); technique corrected; personalised written action plan.
Triggers, smoking and flu vaccine eligibility; recognised the late review against NICE QS25.
Same-day and 999 triggers; teach-back; review booked in two to four weeks.

social.t: Young adults often resist being seen as ill. Frame treatment as what lets him get on with life; one inhaler can feel less medical than two.
Ask whether the attack affected work; a fit note may be needed if recovery is incomplete (self-certification covers the first 7 days).

legal.t: MHRA Drug Safety Update (April 2025): do not prescribe a SABA without a concomitant ICS.

professional.t: NICE QS25 statement 4: general practice follow-up within 2 working days of emergency care for an asthma attack. A late review is a system issue to reflect on and fix (significant event or audit).
GMC Good medical practice (2024): be open when care falls short. Telling him the review should have been sooner builds trust.

community.t: Community pharmacy New Medicine Service for the new inhaler; Asthma + Lung UK technique videos and action plan templates; practice asthma nurse review.

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “Needing A&E and steroids means your asthma was out of control that day. The likely reason is swelling building up while the preventer was on and off, and the cold tipped it over.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the airway lining like a smouldering fire. The preventer keeps it damped down. When it’s taken on and off, the embers build, and a cold is the gust of wind that sets it alight.”

management.reflectIce: “You don’t want asthma to take over your life — that’s exactly what this plan is for.”
management.psychosocial: Use his wish for less fuss: one inhaler, a simple plan, and clear permission to seek help early next time.
sharedPlan: Low-dose MART with ICS/formoterol (NICE NG245); dose and daily maximum per BNF
Technique corrected; personalised written action plan built around a cold as the trigger
Flu vaccine eligibility; triggers and smoking; review the practice recall process
safetyNet: Same day: rising need for extra puffs or relief not lasting
999: struggling to speak, no response to the inhaler
Review in two to four weeks, then regular review

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: The trap is a pleasant, short consultation that agrees with “just a cold”. The marks are in treating the attack as a warning, getting the honest preventer story, and leaving him with a plan he will use.

items.fail: Accepting “it was just a cold” and closing in four minutes.
items.why: NICE NG245 counts any attack needing oral steroids as uncontrolled asthma; missing it is unsafe.
items.fix: One sentence of purpose: “An attack like this is worth understanding so we stop the next one.”

items.fail: Asking “Were you taking your preventer?” in a tone that expects a no.
items.why: “Judgemental approach” feedback; he defends rather than discloses.
items.fix: Normalise first: “Lots of people drift off it when they feel well.”

items.fail: Not asking how long he waited before going to A&E.
items.why: Delayed help-seeking is a recurring factor in asthma deaths (NRAD 2014) and must shape the action plan.
items.fix: “At what point did you decide to get help?” Then build the answer into the plan.

items.fail: Doubling the preventer dose without checking technique or adherence.
items.why: NICE NG245: address adherence and technique before changing medicines.
items.fix: Technique check on camera, then low-dose MART.

items.fail: A generic printed action plan handed over without discussion.
items.why: Action plans work when they are personalised and understood.
items.fix: Use his attack: “A cold plus needing extra puffs is your early warning.”

items.fail: No follow-up date — “see you at your annual review”.
items.why: NICE QS25 expects early follow-up after emergency care; a recent attack needs a close review.
items.fix: Book two to four weeks, and acknowledge this review should have been sooner.
